activities.title: Core Concept: Conditional Bugs & Output Prediction
activities.content:
### Conditional Bugs & Output Prediction

Analyze classic placement traps: accidental assignment (= vs ==), dangling else ambiguity, and missing break bugs.

Conditional code looks deceptively simple, but subtle syntax traps can cause catastrophic bugs that evade automated tests. Interviewers at leading tech firms frequently ask candidates to trace tricky conditional edge cases. Mastering these patterns turns potential pitfalls into easy interview wins.

---

### 1. Accidental Assignment (= vs ==) with Booleans

For numeric types, writing `if (x = 5)` results in a compile error because `int` cannot be converted to `boolean`. However, for boolean variables, writing `if (isAdmin = true)` is **syntactically valid Java**!

```java
boolean isBlocked = false;
if (isBlocked = true) { // BUG: Assigns true to isBlocked and evaluates to true!
    System.out.println("Account blocked!");
}
```

The `=` operator assigns `true` to `isBlocked`, and the assignment expression evaluates to `true`. Always use `==`, or better yet, write `if (isBlocked)` directly without comparisons.

---

### 2. The Stray Semicolon Trap

Placing a semicolon immediately after the `if (...)` statement terminates the conditional branch with an empty statement:

```java
int balance = -50;
if (balance > 0); // BUG: Semicolon ends the if statement right here!
{
    System.out.println("Transfer Approved!"); // ALWAYS EXECUTES!
}
```

The code block in braces becomes an independent unconditioned initializer block and executes regardless of `balance`!

---

### 3. The Dangling Else Problem

When nested `if` statements are written without curly braces, Java compiler binds an `else` to the **closest preceding unmatched if**, regardless of how you indented the code:

```java
int x = 5, y = 15;
if (x > 10)
    if (y > 10)
        System.out.println("Both > 10");
else
    System.out.println("x <= 10"); // DECEPTIVE INDENTATION!
```

Because indentation is ignored by the compiler, the `else` actually pairs with `if (y > 10)`. Since `x > 10` is false, **nothing at all is printed**! Always use curly braces `{}` to enforce clear ownership.

---

### 4. Floating-Point Equality Trap

Due to binary IEEE 754 precision limits, floating point calculations rarely produce exact decimal representations:

```java
double sum = 0.1 + 0.2;
if (sum == 0.3) { // FALSE! sum is 0.30000000000000004
    System.out.println("Equal");
}
```

Always compare floating-point numbers with an epsilon threshold:
`if (Math.abs(sum - 0.3) < 1e-9)`.

---

### 5. String Comparison: `==` vs `.equals()`

Using `==` on Strings checks if both references point to the exact same memory address in the String Pool, NOT whether the text characters match:

```java
String input = new String("PRO");
if (input == "PRO") { // FALSE! Different heap objects
    System.out.println("VIP Access");
}
if (input.equals("PRO")) { // TRUE! Characters match
    System.out.println("VIP Access Approved");
}
```

---

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Takeaway**:
> Always wrap conditional bodies in curly braces, never place a semicolon after an if header, compare Strings using `.equals()`, and compare floating point values with an epsilon tolerance.

questions.prompt: What happens when a semicolon is placed immediately after an if statement header: `if (score > 50);`?
options: A compiler syntax error is generated
The semicolon is treated as an empty statement; the following code block executes unconditionally

The closest preceding unmatched if statement
Whichever if has the matching indentation level
It causes a mandatory compile-time ambiguity error

questions.prompt: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` evaluate to `false` in Java?
options: Because 0.1 and 0.2 are treated as floats while 0.3 is a double
Because binary floating-point representation cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 with exact precision, yielding ~0.30000000000000004

Because Java does not support decimal addition

options: d1.equals(d2)

questions.prompt: Why is `name.equals("admin")` vulnerable to a NullPointerException if `name` is null, and how can it be avoided?
options: Calling any method on a null reference throws NPE; write `"admin".equals(name)` (Yoda condition) instead
It is not vulnerable; Java converts null to "null"
Write `name == "admin"` instead
Use `name != null ? name.equals("admin") : false`
questions.explanation: If `name` is null, `name.equals(...)` throws NPE. Putting the literal first (`"admin".equals(name)`) is null-safe because String literals are never null and safely return false when passed null.

questions.prompt: What compiler error occurs when a non-boolean is used in an if condition: `int status = 1; if (status) { ... }`?
options: NullPointerException
Type mismatch: cannot convert from int to boolean
Operator not applicable
Incompatible operand for condition
questions.explanation: Unlike C or JavaScript where integers (0 vs non-zero) evaluate truthy/falsy, Java is strongly typed and strictly requires an expression that evaluates to a `boolean` in if conditions.

Because braces `{}` were omitted, ONLY `n++;` is guarded by `if (n > 0)`. The next line `n += 5;` is NOT part of the if statement and executes unconditionally. Since n starts at 0, n += 5 sets n to 5. Output: 5.

questions.prompt: What rule should every development team follow to prevent dangling else, stray semicolon, and multi-line omission bugs?
options: Always write conditionals on a single line
Always use explicit curly braces `{}` for every if, else-if, and else block, even for single statements
Never nest conditionals more than one level deep
Use switch statements for all conditionals
questions.explanation: Major style guides (Google Java Style, Oracle) mandate curly braces `{}` for all control flow blocks, even single statements, eliminating an entire class of syntax and indentation bugs.

interviewQA.question: Why does `if (x = 5)` cause a compile error in Java for integers, but `if (flag = true)` compiles without error for booleans?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java is strongly typed. An assignment expression `x = 5` evaluates to the assigned value `5` (an `int`). In Java, `if` statements require a boolean expression, so the compiler rejects an int. However, for a boolean, `flag = true` evaluates to `true` (a `boolean`), which is syntactically valid for an `if` condition. This makes accidental boolean assignment a hazardous silent bug.
keyPoints: Emphasize how Java's strong typing saves us from int assignment bugs, but why booleans require extra vigilance.

interviewQA.question: What is 'Yoda conditions' and why do some developers use them in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: 'Yoda conditions' is a coding style where the constant literal is placed on the left side of the equality check (e.g. `if ("admin".equals(role))` or `if (5 == count)`). In languages like C, this prevented accidental assignment (`if (5 = count)` fails to compile). In Java, writing `"admin".equals(role)` prevents a `NullPointerException` when `role` is null.
keyPoints: Highlight the null-safety benefit of `"literal".equals(variable)` in Java production code.

interviewQA.question: What is the Dangling Else problem and how does Java's grammar resolve it?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The Dangling Else ambiguity arises in nested if statements without braces when an else branch could grammatically belong to either the inner or outer if. Java resolves this by binding the else clause to the closest preceding unmatched if statement in the same block, completely disregarding source code indentation.
keyPoints: Quote the rule: 'Binds to the closest preceding unmatched if'.

interviewQA.question: Why is comparing two doubles with `==` considered a critical code review violation in financial systems?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Binary floating-point arithmetic (IEEE 754) cannot represent most base-10 decimal fractions accurately. Calculations like interest compounding or currency splitting generate minute discrepancies (~0.000000000000004), causing direct equality checks with `==` to fail unpredictably. Financial applications must use `BigDecimal` or integer cents to guarantee precision.
keyPoints: Recommend `BigDecimal` for financial applications to demonstrate real-world enterprise engineering maturity.

interviewQA.question: How can you detect dead or unreachable conditional branches during code review?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Dead code occurs when a branch's condition can never be met due to prior overlapping conditions (e.g. `if (x > 50) ... else if (x > 80)`). While the Java compiler flags compile errors for unconditionally unreachable code (like statements following an unconditional return or `while(false)`), subtle logic overlaps compile without warnings and must be caught via branch-coverage unit tests and careful review of boundary conditions.
keyPoints: Differentiate between compiler-detected unreachable code and logical branch deadlocks.

interviewQA.question: What is the problem with empty if statements: `if (condition);`?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The semicolon immediately following the if condition acts as a null/empty statement. The condition controls only that empty statement, and whatever block follows is executed unconditionally. Linters like Checkstyle and SonarQube flag empty statements as code smells.
keyPoints: Mention static analysis tools like SonarQube and Checkstyle.

interviewQA.question: Why does `String s1 = "hello"; String s2 = new String("hello"); s1 == s2` return false?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `s1` refers to a pooled String literal stored in the String Constant Pool in the JVM heap, while `new String("hello")` explicitly forces the JVM to create a separate distinct object on the regular heap. The `==` operator compares memory references (memory addresses), which differ. `.equals()` must be used to compare character contents.
keyPoints: Reference the String Constant Pool vs Heap object allocation.

interviewQA.question: How can static code analysis tools help teams prevent conditional bugs?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Static analysis tools like SpotBugs, SonarQube, and Error Prone inspect the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) at build time to detect known bug patterns: accidental assignment in conditions, empty if statements, missing break in switch cases, floating-point equality comparisons, and unchecked null dereferences before code ever reaches QA or production.
keyPoints: Mentioning tools like Error Prone and SonarQube proves experience in real CI/CD pipelines.

interviewQA.question: Can an `else` branch exist without an accompanying `if`?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. An `else` keyword without a preceding `if` statement causes a compile-time syntax error: `'else' without 'if'`. Every `else` must have a corresponding `if` to which it attaches.
keyPoints: Straightforward syntax question — answer cleanly and concisely.
